title: Rank-based cache
label: idb
statement:
Create a cache with:

• fixed capacity
• static distinct integer ranks
• key/value
• slow DataSource

If cache is full:

evict the item with the lowest rank.

If the requested item is not cached:

retrieve from DataSource.
provenance: Supplied by you from InterviewDB — the statement above is **verbatim**. Corroboration: InterviewDB + a first-hand report of an LFU cache with GetRank().
clarify: `GetRank(key)` is cheap and available without fetching the value.
A low-ranked newcomer is **not** cached when the cache is full.

flaw.ctx: You asked for an LRU cache. It passes put-then-get.
flaw.answer: **Get never moves the node to the front**, so reads do not count as use. Put 1, put 2, get 1, put 3 → key 1 (just read) is evicted. Passes put/get tests; fails the first eviction-after-read test.
flaw.fix: Move the node to the front in Get, exactly as Put does.

qa.a: Red-black tree: O(log n) insert, remove, lookup; in-order enumeration.

qa.q: How do you get a floor (largest ≤ x)?
qa.a: `GetViewBetween(min, x).Max` — O(log n). There is no `floorKey` like Java's TreeMap.
O(1) average for lookup, insert, remove; O(n) worst case if many keys collide. Enumeration is O(n) and order is not guaranteed.

Separate chaining, but without node objects: an `int[] buckets` of indices into an `Entry[]` array, each entry carrying its hash, key, value and a `next` index. Colliding keys form a chain through `next`.

When the entries array is full it grows to a larger prime (about double) and every entry is rehashed into new buckets — O(n) for that insert, amortised O(1). Pre-size with the constructor capacity when you know n.
Removing does not shrink anything: freed slots go on a free list for reuse. `TrimExcess()` shrinks. A struct key that is large is copied into every entry.

Only code that locks the *same object*. `lock (x)` is `Monitor.Enter/Exit` on x's object header, in a try/finally. It also acts as a full memory barrier, so writes inside are visible to the next locker.
Yes, with two locks taken in different orders (D5), or with a call out to unknown code while holding the lock. One lock and no callouts cannot deadlock. `Monitor` is re-entrant for the same thread.

Uncontended, a lock is tens of nanoseconds. Contended, threads spin briefly then block, causing context switches; throughput collapses toward one thread's worth. The fix is less work under the lock, or more locks (striping).
`this`, a `Type`, a string — other code can lock them too. Use a private readonly object (or `System.Threading.Lock` in .NET 9+).

learn.title: 1 · Problem
learn.md:
> Create a cache with:
> 
> • fixed capacity
> • static distinct integer ranks
> • key/value
> • slow DataSource
> 
> If cache is full:
> 
> evict the item with the lowest rank.
> 
> If the requested item is not cached:
> 
> retrieve from DataSource.

A cache in front of something slow, where importance is given rather than inferred. Unlike LRU or LFU, the cache is told what each item is worth and never has to guess.

`Get(key)` returns the value, from the cache if present and from the source otherwise. The design content is the eviction and admission policy around it.

learn.title: 2 · Clarifications
learn.md:
The interesting gap: **what happens when the new item’s rank is lower than everything in the cache?**

Taken literally, "if the cache is full, evict the lowest rank" would have you evict a better item and store a worse one — and if the next request is for that same low-ranked key, you would do it again, thrashing the cache with the least valuable data. That is clearly not intended, but the statement does not rule it out.

I **decline to cache** in that case and return the value anyway, which is an admission policy rather than an eviction policy, and I would say so explicitly. It is the single best thing to raise on this question, because it is a real design decision hiding in an under-specified sentence.

Also unstated: is rank available without a fetch? `GetRank(key)` as a separate method implies yes, which matters — if rank were only known *after* the expensive fetch, you could not decide admission before paying for the data.

| Assumption | If it is wrong |
|---|---|
| `GetRank(key)` is cheap and available without fetching the value. | If rank came only with the data, admission could not be decided before paying the fetch cost — the policy would have to become "fetch, then decide whether to keep", which is still correct but much less useful. |
| A low-ranked newcomer is **not** cached when the cache is full. | The literal reading would evict something better to store something worse. This is the clarification to raise. |
| Ranks really are distinct. | **The comparer depends on it.** Comparing on rank alone means two items with equal rank look identical to the sorted set, and one would be silently dropped. If ranks could collide, the comparer must fall back to the key. |
| No TTL, no invalidation. | With static ranks and immutable values there is nothing to expire. If values could change behind the cache, this becomes Q1 and needs a TTL or an invalidation hook. |

learn.title: 3 · Key insight
learn.md:
Two observations, and the first one is a gift you should notice out loud.

**Static ranks remove the hard part of LFU.** In an LFU cache, every access changes a key’s frequency, so the priority structure must support "increase the priority of this arbitrary element", which a plain heap cannot do in better than O(n). That is why LFU needs the bucket-of-equal-counts construction from `432 All O’one`. Here, rank never changes. So nothing is ever re-prioritised, and a simple ordered structure is enough. Saying "this is much easier than LFU, and here is exactly why" is a strong opening.

**Distinct ranks let you compare on rank alone.** The eviction victim is the minimum rank, so you need a structure that yields its minimum cheaply, plus a dictionary for O(1) lookup by key. Same pairing as Q1 and Q12: one structure for the ordering, one for the lookup.

A min-heap gives O(1) peek and O(log n) pop. A `SortedSet` gives O(log n) minimum and, unlike a heap, supports removing an arbitrary element — which a heap cannot do without an auxiliary index. Since nothing here needs arbitrary removal yet, either works; the sorted set costs nothing extra and keeps the door open.

And then the third thing, which the statement does not ask and which is the actual design judgement: **eviction policy and admission policy are different questions.** "Evict the lowest rank" says what leaves. It does not say what is allowed in. If a newcomer ranks below everything held, admitting it means evicting something better — so the right policy is to serve the value and not cache it. Recognising that an under-specified sentence conceals a second policy is the staff-level move here.

learn.title: 4 · Approach
learn.md:
**Brute force.** A `Dictionary<TKey, (value, rank)>`. On a miss when full, scan every entry to find the lowest rank and evict it. *`Get` O(1) on a hit, O(capacity) on an eviction. Space O(capacity).*

**Why not good enough.** At capacity 100 the scan is irrelevant and this is a perfectly good answer to give first. It stops being fine at capacity 100,000 — and more importantly, it is the same self-defeating shape as Q1’s brute force: the larger you make the cache to improve the hit rate, the more each miss costs. A structure that knows its own minimum removes that coupling.

**The approach.**

| Stage | What happens |
|---|---|
| INPUT | `Get(key)`, a capacity, and an `IRankedDataSource` |
| TRANSFORMATION | Each entry is stored twice: by key for lookup, and by rank for eviction |
| DATA STRUCTURE | `Dictionary<TKey, (TValue, int)>` plus `SortedSet<(int Rank, TKey Key)>` with a rank-only comparer |
| ALGORITHM | Hit → return. Miss → fetch, then admit only if the rank beats the current minimum; admitting evicts the minimum. |
| OUTPUT | The value, always; caching is a separate decision |

learn.title: 5 · Why the approach works
learn.md:
- `Get`: dictionary hit → count it and return.
- Miss → fetch the value and the rank from the source.
- If the cache is not full, store and index it.
- If full, compare the new rank with `_byRank.Min.Rank`.
- Lower → count a rejection and return the value **without caching**.
- Higher → evict the minimum from both structures, then store and index the newcomer.

- Ranks are **static** — they never change for a key. This is what makes a heap or sorted set viable, because nothing ever needs re-prioritising.
- Ranks are **distinct**, so comparing on rank alone is a total order.
- Fixed capacity; eviction is by lowest rank.
- The data source is slow, so a miss is expensive and the hit rate is the thing being optimised.

learn.title: 6 · Data structures
learn.md:
| Structure | Why |
|---|---|
| `Dictionary` for lookup | O(1) hit path, which is the whole reason a cache exists. |
| `SortedSet<(int Rank, TKey Key)>` for eviction order | O(log n) minimum and O(log n) arbitrary removal. A `PriorityQueue` would give a cheaper peek and **cannot remove an arbitrary element**, which forecloses the invalidation follow-up. The sorted set costs a log factor on peek and keeps the option. |
| A comparer on **rank only** | Avoids requiring `TKey : IComparable`, which would be an unnecessary constraint on the cache’s users. Safe **because ranks are distinct** — and if that guarantee failed, the comparer would silently drop entries, which is the thing to flag. |
| Admission check before eviction | The policy decision. Comparing the newcomer’s rank against the current minimum is one line and it is what stops the cache being thrashed by low-value keys. |
| Counters for hits, misses, admissions and rejections | A cache you cannot observe is a cache you cannot tune. Four increments, and they turn "is the policy working" from an argument into a measurement. |

learn.title: 7 · C# implementation — walkthrough
learn.md:
**The `ByRank` comparer, and the guarantee it leans on.** It compares `a.Rank.CompareTo(b.Rank)` and ignores the key. A `SortedSet` treats "compares equal" as "is the same element", so two entries with the same rank would collapse and one would be silently lost. **Distinct ranks are what make this safe**, and the comment says so in the code. If the guarantee were dropped, the comparer would need `?: a.Key.CompareTo(b.Key)` and `TKey` would have to be comparable.

**Why the value is returned even when not cached.** `Get` fetches, calls `Admit`, and returns the value regardless of what `Admit` decided. Caching is an optimisation, not part of the contract — conflating the two is how a cache ends up unable to serve keys it has chosen not to store.

**`if (rank < lowest.Rank) { Rejected++; return; }`.** The admission policy, in one line. Everything before it is mechanism; this is the judgement. Note `<` rather than `<=`: an equal rank cannot occur given the distinctness guarantee, so the choice is moot — but writing `<` rather than `<=` means the code would prefer the incumbent on a tie, which is the conservative behaviour.

**Eviction touches both structures.** `_byRank.Remove(lowest)` and `_entries.Remove(lowest.Key)`. The invariant is that the two hold the same key set at all times, and the tuple in the sorted set carries the key precisely so the dictionary entry can be found from it — the same reason Q1’s node carries its key.

**The four counters.** `Hits`, `Misses`, `Admitted`, `Rejected`. The last two are the ones that matter for this design: a high rejection count means capacity is too small for the rank distribution, and that is not visible from the hit rate alone. It is two lines of code and it is the difference between a policy you can tune and one you can only argue about.

**`LowestRank` as a public property.** Exposed for tests, and useful in production for the same reason — it is the admission threshold, so it answers "what rank do I need to get cached right now".

learn.title: 8 · Complexity
learn.md:
| Operation | Time | Space | Why |
|---|---|---|---|
| `Get` (hit) | O(1) expected | O(1) | One dictionary probe |
| `Get` (miss, not full) | O(log n) | O(1) | Source fetch plus one sorted-set insert |
| `Get` (miss, admitted) | O(log n) | O(1) | One `Min`, one remove, one insert |
| `Get` (miss, rejected) | O(log n) | O(1) | One `Min`, then nothing |
| space | — | O(capacity) | One dictionary entry and one set entry per cached key |

**The source fetch dominates everything on this table and it is worth saying so.** A slow data source is by definition orders of magnitude above a log-n in-memory operation, so optimising O(log n) to O(1) here would be pointless. What matters is the **hit rate**, which is a function of the policy rather than of the data structures — which is why the admission decision deserves more of the discussion than the choice between a heap and a sorted set.

learn.title: 9 · Edge cases
learn.md:
| Case | Behaviour |
|---|---|
| Capacity 0 or negative | Throws in the constructor. |
| First `Get` on an empty cache | Miss, fetch, store. No eviction path taken. |
| Cache full, newcomer ranks highest | Minimum evicted, newcomer admitted. |
| Cache full, newcomer ranks lowest | **Not admitted**; value still returned. The design decision. |
| Repeated request for a rejected key | Every one is a miss. The cost of the policy, and a counter makes it visible. |
| Same key requested twice | Second is a hit; the source is called once. |
| Equal ranks, despite the guarantee | The comparer would treat them as one entry and silently lose one. Flag it — the code depends on the guarantee the statement gave. |
| Source throws | Propagates. The cache is unchanged, because nothing is stored until the fetch succeeds. |
| Capacity 1 | Works: every miss with a higher rank replaces the single entry. |

learn.title: 16 · Follow-up questions
learn.md:
**Ranks are no longer static — they change as items are accessed. Now what?**

A heap cannot increase the priority of an arbitrary element without an index into it, and a `SortedSet` needs remove-then-reinsert, O(log n) per access — on the **hit** path, which was O(1). That is the real cost: the hot path gets slower.

The proper answer is the `432 All O’one` construction: a doubly linked list of count buckets, each bucket holding the keys with that count, plus a map from key to its bucket. Incrementing a count is unlinking from one bucket and linking into the adjacent one — O(1). The minimum is the head bucket. That is also how LFU caches are built, and the reported LinkedIn question adds LRU ordering *within* a bucket, which the bucket’s own list gives you for free.

*Trade-off:* O(1) everything, for considerably more code and a structure that is genuinely fiddly to get right. With static ranks none of it is needed, which is exactly why the word "static" in the statement is worth acknowledging — it is the difference between this question and a Hard one.

**Combine rank with recency, so a low-ranked but very hot key can still be cached.**

Score each entry as a function of both, for example `rank + w · recencyBonus`, and evict the lowest score. Or segment the cache: reserve most of the capacity for rank-ordered entries and a small window for recently-requested ones, promoting a key out of the window if it is requested again. The segmented approach is what production caches actually do — it is the shape of both ARC and W-TinyLFU.

*Trade-off:* A combined score makes the priority dynamic, so the previous follow-up’s problem arrives with it. Segmentation keeps each structure simple and static, at the cost of a tuning parameter — how big the window is — which nobody can set correctly without measurement. I would segment, and instrument it, and let the rejection counter tell me the window size.

**It is distributed across many nodes.**

Partition by key with consistent hashing; each node runs this cache over its own shard. Eviction becomes per-shard, so the item evicted is the lowest rank **on that node**, not globally. Ranks being static helps enormously here — they need no coordination or replication, so every node can decide independently and no node ever disagrees with another about an item’s worth.

*Trade-off:* Per-shard eviction is approximate: a globally high-ranked item can be evicted because its shard happens to be full of even better items. That is the same approximation as sharded LRU and it is universally accepted. Static ranks make this the easiest distributed cache of the three on this page, and that is worth saying.

**Values can change in the source. Keep the cache correct.**

Either a TTL per entry, which is Q1 and composes directly, or an explicit `Invalidate(key)` that removes from both structures. **This is where the choice of `SortedSet` over `PriorityQueue` pays off**: arbitrary removal is O(log n) on a sorted set and impossible on a heap without an auxiliary index.

*Trade-off:* TTL is self-healing and serves stale data for up to the TTL. Explicit invalidation is exact and needs the source to notify the cache, which is a coupling that does not always exist. Most systems use both — invalidation where a signal exists, TTL as the backstop — and saying that is better than picking one.

**Level 1 — Correctness**

- *What are the edge cases — empty, duplicates, missing values, invalid input?* — Names them and says what the code does for each

**Level 2 — Complexity**

- *Time and space complexity? Can it be improved? What happens as N grows?* — States both, names the bottleneck
